1. # **INTRODUCTION** {#introduction}

   1. ## **Background of the Study** {#background-of-the-study}

Lost and found systems began as simple, informal collections of misplaced items in public areas which provided a centralized method for retrieving misplaced belongings. Over time, these systems had evolved into more structured and institutionalized methods, especially within schools, offices and public transportation (Hall, 2024). Modern lost and found systems aim to address the universal problem of lost belongings among campus goers by providing an organized and efficient method for item retrieval. Unlike traditional approaches such as notice boards and manual logbooks which are time-consuming, inconsistent and prone to human error, an intelligent multimodal Lost and Found System offers numerous advantages (Vasavi et al., 2022). It provides faster and more accurate item matching, ensures better organization of lost and found records and it enhances user convenience through digital accessibility. Additionally, it promotes transparency, reduces the risk of misplaced reports and increases the chances of reuniting owners with their lost belongings efficiently (Reunitus, 2025).

Attempts to automate lost and found processes have moved towards digital solutions that use image-based matching algorithms. Although helpful in some cases, these methods struggled to cope with variable lighting, cluttered backgrounds, and changes in object viewpoint, resulting in unreliable matches when conditions were less controlled (Bartol et al., 2020). With the introduction of deep learning-based image recognition, accuracy and efficiency improved significantly. Modern models for object identification and item matching, such as MobileNetV2 enhanced with attention modules, now allow systems to focus on the most meaningful image features and produce better results even for visually similar objects. (Zhou et al., 2023). Nevertheless, systems relying solely on images cannot help when students are unable to provide a photo of their missing item.

The limitations of existing visual-based retrieval systems such as their dependency on user-provided images which are not always available, its quality, lighting conditions, and angle variations, have hindered their effectiveness in accurately identifying and matching items. To address these challenges this lost and found system leverages Fine-Grained CLIP (FGCLIP) by Xie et al. (2025) in the text-to-image matching branch. FGCLIP enhances the alignment between images and textual descriptions by combining long-caption augmentation, region level grounding, and hard-negative sampling, enabling the model to preserve and use subtle visual details. This fine-grained alignment is especially beneficial for lost and found applications, where differentiating between similar objects is critical to improving item retrieval accuracy.

Beyond appearance-based matching, spatio-temporal filtering which considers where and when items were reported lost or found can serve as an additional layer of verification (Al Hassan et al., 2020). Even if the item descriptions are vague or the images slightly unclear, the overlap in time and location significantly increases the likelihood of a correct match. Incorporating such spatio-temporal checks reduces false claims, strengthens security, and ensures that only legitimate owners are alerted about possible matches (Silva & Sichman, 2022).

By integrating both image-to-image and text-to-image approaches, reinforced with spatio-temporal verification, a multimodal lost and found system can overcome the limitations of single-modality approaches, reduce mismatches, improve retrieval accuracy and provide a more efficient way to return items to their rightful owners, particularly within schools and campuses. Moreover, the system can now be fully automated, where students who report missing items are automatically notified via email once a potential match is found. This feature minimizes the need for repeated office visits or constant manual checking, streamlining the recovery process and making lost-and-found retrieval more accessible, secure, and user-friendly.

2. ## **Objectives of the Study** {#objectives-of-the-study}

To develop an automated multimodal lost and found system for campuses that integrates image-to-image matching, and text-to-image retrieval enhancing the accuracy, fairness, and efficiency of lost item recovery.

The specific objectives follow:

1. To evaluate image recognition accuracy using MobileNetV2 by measuring:  
   1. mAP (Mean Average Precision)  
      2. Precision@K (R@1, R@5, R@10)  
      3. Recall@K (R@1, R@5, R@10)  
      4. Confusion Matrix

2. To assess the cross-modal retrieval performance of FGCLIP for matching text descriptions to image using:

   1. Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)

      2. Recall@K (R@1, R@5, R@10)

      3. Confusion Matrix

3. To measure System Performance and Feasibility for Real-World Deployment utilizing:

   1. Average and Peak Query Response Time (Latency)

      2. Queries Per Second (QPS) / Maximum Concurrent Users

      3. CPU and Memory Resource Utilization

   3. ## **Significance of the Study** {#significance-of-the-study}

**Students**. This system provides students with an efficient way of both reporting and locating lost items. With the help of both image and text input, students can easily search for their lost items without relying on vague descriptions, saving time and reducing stress.

**School Personnel.** This system minimizes the manual work of managing lost and found items. Maintaining order and accuracy in tracking, storing, and returning lost items will be much easier and better, allowing school personnel to focus more on academic and administrative duties.

**School Administration.** This system promotes organization, accountability, and digital transformation in school operations due to its systematic and technology-driven nature. Adopting this system will enhance student services and promote security within the campus which will make the student experience better.

**Future Researchers.** This study will serve as a reference for future projects that utilizes artificial intelligence, image processing, and multimodal search technologies in campus-based systems. 

4. ## **Scope and Delimitations** {#scope-and-delimitations}

The development of this Lost and Found platform focuses on aiding users in reporting lost and found items mainly within a campus. Users can provide information through uploading images of items or submitting detailed text descriptions. The core innovation of the system lies in enabling text-to-image search, where natural language is interpreted and compared against stored images using advanced deep learning models such as FGCLIP, MobileNetV2, and the CBAM module. This feature solves the common limitation of existing systems, where retrieval is solely based on text which is often unreliable. To add to the text-to-image search, the platform also supports image-to-image search, allowing users to to upload an image and retrieve visually similar items. Furthermore, the platform incorporates basic functionalities such as user registration, item posting, and basic moderation.

The system’s performance will be evaluated strictly as a web-based application accessed through desktop or laptop computers. Testing will be conducted on workstations equipped with Intel Core i5/i7 or AMD Ryzen processors, 8GB to 16GB of RAM, and NVIDIA GPUs (GTX 1050 Ti or RTX 3060\) to handle the AI processing. To ensure consistent speed and response times, all tests will use a stable Fiber or LAN internet connection, explicitly excluding performance issues caused by slow Wi-Fi or unstable mobile data. Furthermore, the system’s ability to handle multiple users will be tested up to a maximum of 100 concurrent requests running on the Python 3.10 framework.

The platform is designed exclusively for use within the campus grounds and will not handle lost and found cases outside of it. Inputs will be limited to English language, and the system will primarily focus on visually identifiable items. Non-distinguishable items such as money, generic flash drives, or documents without unique marks may not be effectively searchable. The platform will also not include automated item handover features and will not be developed as a native mobile application, but will instead be accessible through desktop and mobile web browsers. The accuracy of text-to-image matching is subject to factors such as quality of user-inputted descriptions, the content of the dataset, and the performance constraints of the models used.

2. # **CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK** {#conceptual-framework}

   1. ## **Review of Related Literature** {#review-of-related-literature}

Lost and found systems have evolved technologically in recent years, moving away from standard centralized databases towards multimodal and intelligent systems. Recent studies have explored approaches integrating text descriptions and images to improve the efficiency and    accuracy of retrieving lost items. This section reviews prominent literary works that highlight the current state of research regarding automated lost and found identification.

Nama and Putri (2021) aimed to digitize lost item reporting at MARA Technological University (UiTM). It introduced a digital platform that centralized the reporting and tracking of lost belongings through an Android application connected to a Firebase database, aiming to modernize the university’s lost and found management process.

This study uses a mobile application to digitize lost item reporting at MARA Technological University (UiTM) through an android app supported by firebase database. The system enhanced accessibility and organization by allowing users to conveniently submit and browse reports, replacing manual logbooks. However, its reliance on text and image uploads without automated matching or similarity detection, along with a basic keyword-based search and Android-only availability, limited its search accuracy and overall accessibility.

Building upon digital lost and found systems, the “AUFound” system developed by Castro et al. (2022) for Angeles University Foundation aimed to enhance manual-based record management by developing a dual-platform solution where students can submit reports via a mobile application, while administrators could manage item inventory through a web-based portal. The system sought to enhance efficiency, accessibility and organization by digitizing the reporting process and providing an easier way to manage item records.

This study demonstrates notable strengths such as improving efficiency and accessibility by replacing manual logbooks with a digital dual platform system that allowed students to report lost items through a mobile app and administrators to manage records via a web portal which enhances organization and streamlined record management. However, the system’s main weakness lay in its reliance on basic text-based reporting and limited search functionality, lacking advanced features such as image recognition, filtering or intelligent search capabilities, which could have improved accuracy and user experience.

Cartago et al. (2023) developed a similar system to serve as a centralized database for searching lost items. This web-based system was built primarily using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, and a MySQL database managed via XAMPP. Like AUFound, the system helped simplify the process through a digital platform. 

The strength of this study introduces a web-based lost and found system designed as a centralized database for managing and searching lost items, one of its strengths lies in simplifying the reporting and retrieval process through a digital platform, making it more efficient and accessible than the traditional ones. The use of familiar web technologies such as HTML, CSS, Javascript, PHP and MYSQL also made the system practical and easy to maintain. However, the study’s main weakness was its reliance on basic text matching and CRUD operations which limited the search accuracy. This approach could overlook relevant results when users used different terms or phrasing, reducing the overall effectiveness of the system.

Prawira and Saputri (2024) developed a model that integrates image comparison and string matching for lost item identification. The model utilized the RestNet-50 architecture and a convolutional neural network (CNN) for image feature extraction, then using Euclidean distance, measures image similarity based on the numerical distance between feature vectors extracted from the images. Additionally, the paper also utilized Natural Language Processing (NLP) to pre-process textual descriptions. The descriptions are converted into vector representations and compared using cosine similarity (angle between vectors) to determine relatedness.

With this multimodal approach, the study was able to resolve ambiguity between visually similar items by using text descriptions. Results showed a high accuracy of 97.92% for the model’s text matching component, demonstrating effectiveness in handling user provided descriptions. Despite its exceptional performance in text analysis, the system yielded a lower accuracy for image matching in comparison, with an accuracy of 29.96%. This result is highly attributed to a very limited dataset which only consisted of 4 specific item categories (smartphones, cameras, glasses, and hats) which ultimately contributed to its poor performance with image matching.  The authors stated that scaling up the retraining the model was necessary for improvement and recommended increasing the dataset in future works. 

Zhou et al. (2023) proposed LostNet, an intelligent lost and found image identification system. It utilized a MobileNetV2 model combined with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to improve feature focus. The model was trained with transfer learning (reusing a pre-trained model for a new, related task) and data augmentation (creating modified copies of existing data to expand a training set) on a dataset of 10 lost item categories. It also used a perceptual hash algorithm to generate a unique hash value for each image which acts as a “fingerprint” to be used for image similarity searching. 

During testing, LostNet achieved 96.8% accuracy and demonstrated low computational requirements, capable of running on standard hardware. Its lightweight architecture also makes it practical and scalable. However, the system is primarily image-based with no text search functionality, and because of its limitation to only 10 predefined categories, objects that fall outside of this scope may be misidentified. Furthermore, it does not apply advanced image pre-processing beyond basic scaling, which could lead to information loss or distortion, affecting classification accuracy and recognition performance due to uneven image quality and resolution. The researchers acknowledged these limitations and recommended expanding categories, fine-tuning datasets, and better image pre-processing.

The seminal work by Radford et al. (2021) demonstrated a significant advancement towards multimodal research. The paper introduced CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), a model that learns visual concepts by being trained on a data set of 400 million image-text pairs from the internet. The model learns to associate a wide range of visual concepts with their textual descriptions by pulling their digital representations (embeddings) together in a shared conceptual space. An image encoder and text encoder are jointly trained to predict the correct pairings of images and text. 

This approach enables zero-shot learning, which is the ability of the model to recognize new categories without specific training. This allows it to be flexible and capable of performing a wider range of visual tasks without additional training data. A crucial drawback of the model is CLIP’s inability to handle fine-grained distinctions (subtle differences between similar items). While it performs exceptionally well with basic object recognition,  a critical limitation of the original model is that it often fails to differentiate between visually similar objects. This poses a crucial challenge with accurate image matching.

A study by Mikhalvich et. al. (2023) presented an image search engine built on OpenAI’s CLIP model, packaged as a command-line tool called rclip. This tool uses CLIP’s ability to convert images and natural language queries into vector embeddings, allowing zero-shot image retrieval without the need for labeled datasets. To optimize performance, the system employs an SQLite database for caching image embeddings, allowing for efficient repeated searches with search times ranging from 4 seconds for 50,000 images to 11 seconds for over 1.28 million images on an Apple M1 Max CPU. The tool achieved 55.51% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 datasets but showed limited fine-grained accuracy with 32.27% on ImageNet1k. 

This study showcases several strengths particularly its innovative use of OpenAI’s Clip model for zero shot image retrieval without requiring labeled datasets. Its integration with an SQLite database for caching image embeddings greatly improved efficiency, enabling quick search time even with large datasets. The system also demonstrated practical scalability and strong performance for general image retrieval tasks. However, the study also had its weaknesses, including limited fine-grained accuracy, as shown by its lower performance on the ImageNet1k dataset. Additionally, it required re-indexing when image file paths changed and loaded unnecessary model components during searches, which reduced efficiency and flexibility in real-world applications.

Xie et al. (2025) introduced Fine-Grained CLIP (FG-CLIP), a model designed to enhance CLIP's ability to recognize subtle visuals through a data-centric, two-stage training approach. The authors first generated 1.6 billion detailed captions using Large Multimodal Models to enrich global semantic context. They then developed FineHARD, a dataset of 12 million images with 40 million region-specific annotations and 10 million "hard negative" samples, misleading captions that help model learn the fine distinctions, By combining both global and regional contrastive learning, FG-CLIP achieved significant improvements over the original CLIP.

The strength of FG-CLIP is in its comprehensive data-driven design and innovative training methodology, which allow it to capture nuanced visual features that standard CLIP models often miss. The combination of large-scale descriptive data generation and region-level supervision results in great accuracy and fine-detail recognition. However, the model's primary limitation is its dependence on massive computational power and data resources. The scale of its dataset and training process makes FG-CLIP difficult to reproduce or deploy in environments with limited infrastructure, restricting its accessibility and practical application.

The study Dhanawardhana et al. (2025) developed, titled “Enhancing Lost and Found Systems with Multi-Modal Deep Learning: Integrating SBERT and Siamese Networks” focuses on enhancing the accuracy in lost and found systems through multi-modal matching. The model combined the use of both text-to-image and image-to image matching and integrated Sentence-BERT (SBERT) for semantic text encoding and a Siamese Network powered by MobileNetV2 for image similarity detection. Additionally, the system incorporated contextual metadata such as location and time to enhance the precision of item identification, achieving a high F1 score of 0.98, indicating a strong overall performance.

The main strength of Dhanawardhana et al's (2025) study lies in its effective combination of textual and visual data, which significantly enhances the reliability of lost and found item matching. The integration of SBERT and Siamese Network model shows a strong capability of understanding bit semantic meaning and visual similarity resulting in high accuracy. However, despite its performance, the system has a couple of limitations. It needed significant computational resources, making real-time implementation and large-scale deployment challenging.

**Image Processing Standards**

	Re-examining the work of Zhou et al. (2024) from a preprocessing lens, it employs OpenCV for image normalization and feature preparation in LostNet, ensuring robustness to minor distortions such as brightness shifts while maintaining 96.8% accuracy on edge hardware. A key achievement of the study is validating OpenCV as a lightweight, deterministic, and computationally efficient preprocessing tool that standardizes images and reduces noise without introducing significant latency. The strength of OpenCV lies in its hardware-agnostic operations and minimal memory overhead, making it well suited for real-time and resource-constrained deployments. However, its reliance on low-level, handcrafted transformations limits semantic understanding, and OpenCV-based preprocessing is less effective in handling complex variations such as occlusion and viewpoint changes.

	Bansal and Parashar (2021) employs Pillow (PIL fork) for image loading, resizing, and normalization within a web-based content-based image retrieval system, demonstrating its effectiveness as a reliable and developer-friendly preprocessing library for deep learning pipelines. A key achievement of the study is validating Pillow’s ability to provide consistent image formatting and resolution standardization that integrates seamlessly with pretrained CNNs such as VGG16, enabling accurate semantic retrieval across diverse object categories. The strength of Pillow lies in its simplicity, portability, and tight integration with Python-based web frameworks, which makes it well suited for rapid development and server-side preprocessing. However, Pillow’s functionality is largely limited to basic image transformations, offering minimal support for advanced photometric normalization or robustness-oriented preprocessing. As a result, PIL-based preprocessing is less effective in handling illumination variations, noise, and other real-world distortions compared to more specialized computer vision libraries such as OpenCV.

**Deep Learning Computational Frameworks**

To support the neural network requirements of this study, the researchers utilized Pytorch, a deep learning library formally introduced by Paszke et al. (2019). Traditional frameworks rely on static graph declarations that require the entire model structure to be fixed before running while PyTorch employs an “imperative programming model” which allows tensor operations to be executed immediately as they are written. This design enables “define-by-run” execution, where the computational graph is constructed dynamically at runtime. This provides the flexibility necessary for complex, dynamic architectures such as the Transformers used in the FG-CLIP. Furthermore, the literature highlights that PyTorch was designed to integrate smoothly with standard Python tools and provides efficient hardware acceleration, ensuring that heavy data processing tasks can be performed on modern graphical processing units (GPUs). However, its reliance on dynamic execution and the Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) can introduce runtime latency compared to static graph frameworks (like Caffe or TensorFlow), which compile the entire computation graph ahead of time for optimized production scalability.

Images preprocessing and computer vision operations in this study were handled using Torchvision, a library within the Pytorch ecosystem that supplies widely used datasets, pretrained model  architectures, and image transformation tools for deep learning applications. The library supports feature extraction and transfer learning through established convolutional neural network (CNN) models. It also provides a broad range of image preprocessing and data augmentation functions, including resizing, cropping, normalization and tensor conversion, all of which are fully compatible with PyTorch tensors. These capabilities have been shown to facilitate effective fine-grained image classification and model evaluation in recent studies (Albardi et al., 2021). This integration enables efficient incorporation of visual data pipelines into the training and inference procedures of the FG-CLIP framework. As a result, Torchvision contributes to reliable, reproducible and GPU-accelerated processing of visual data. However, Torchvision can be limited in terms of supporting very specialized or custom image processing workflows, which may require additional coding or integration with other libraries to meet highly specific research requirements. 

In a computational view, Bansa and Parasharl (2021), their Lost and Found Project uses NumPy arrays to store and manipulate high-dimensional VGG16 feature vectors, enabling rapid cosine similarity computations and top-k retrieval for matching user-uploaded lost item images against a database. A key strength of the study is demonstrating NumPy as a lightweight, deterministic, and computationally efficient tool for feature storage and vectorized operations, allowing scalable retrieval on standard hardware without specialized resources. However, NumPy’s lack of native GPU acceleration constrains large-scale similarity searches, and manual array blending introduces potential overflow risks, requiring careful dtype management or supplementation with libraries such as OpenCV for robust pixel-level processing.

2. ## **Concept of the Study (*major steps of the study)*** {#concept-of-the-study-(major-steps-of-the-study)}

| ![][image1] |
| :---: |

**Figure 2-1 Concept of the Study of the Proposed Multimodal Retrieval System**

Figure 2-1 illustrates the conceptual framework of the proposed multimodal retrieval system. The system processes both images and text input to perform retrieval tasks. For images, the workflow begins with preprocessing (resizing and normalization), followed by feature extraction using the MobileNetV2 image encoder to generate image embeddings, these image embeddings are then compared with the image embeddings of the lost and found items in the system’s database through cosine similarity. For text input, the text is first preprocessed and tokenized, then encoded using FG-CLIP to generate text embeddings, these are also compared against the image embedding within the database. The similarity scores obtained from both image to image and text to image matching are subsequently refined through spatio-temporal filtering, which incorporates location proximity and time constraints to improve the relevance and accuracy of the retrieved items. Based on the filtered similarity scores, the system generates a query result, which consists of the top-matching lost or found items ranked according to their relevance to the input query. Then output  Finally, the system is evaluated using metrics such as precision, recall, accuracy, confusion matrix, mean reciprocal rank, and cosine similarity to assess the performance of the retrieval tasks.

| ![][image2] |
| :---: |

**Figure 2-2: Lost and Found System Literature Map**  
Figure 2-2 presents a literature mapping of lost and found systems, highlighting the different approaches in retrieval and fusion methods. The first category, Image-to-Image, focuses on visual similarity matching, including methods like LostNet (Zhou et al., 2024\) and TF-IDF cosine similarity approaches. The Text-to-Text category involves text-based matching systems, while Fusion Text-to-Text with Image-to-Image integrates both modalities to improve semantic understanding, as in recent multi-modal deep learning frameworks. Cross-modal/Text-to-Image Retrieval methods are divided into dual-encoder contrastive approaches (CLIP-style) and cross-modal interaction methods that optimize alignment and interaction between text and image embeddings. Lastly, Image-to-Image and Text-Image Fusion Methods employ modal fusion techniques for combined retrieval tasks, leveraging graph-based fusion or pre-trained transfer learning models. This figure illustrates the evolution of techniques and the diversity of strategies used in lost-and-found retrieval systems.

3. ## **Definition of Terms** {#definition-of-terms}

**Multimodal Deep Learning**	 	In the context of this study, Multimodal Deep Learning refers to the system’s integration of two distinct neural networks to process different types of user queries independently. Specifically, it utilizes FG-CLIP to interpret the semantics of natural language descriptions for text-to-image search, while employing MobileNetV2 to identify visually similar items from uploaded reference photos for image-to-image search. This approach is defined as “Multimodal” as it enables the system to accept and interpret both textual and visual inputs allowing users to search based on available information.

**Model** 	 	A "model" refers to a specific, trained machine learning algorithm that performs a key task. Several were utilized, including MobileNetV2 as our image encoder and FG-CLIP as our text encoder. These models are the computational engines of our system, responsible for processing raw data (images and text) and converting it into searchable representations (embeddings). 

**Attention**	It specifically refers to the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which enhances our MobileNetV2 model. This is a technical mechanism within the neural network that allows it to dynamically weigh the importance of different features in an image. 

**Semantic**	The underlying meaning of the data, beyond just surface-level keywords. The text encoder is designed to capture the semantic content of a user's description. This ability to match based on meaning, not just identical words, is a key advantage of our approach.

**Fine-Grained**	It describes the model's ability to recognize and differentiate between objects based on subtle, highly specific details, rather than just broad categories. 

**Architecture**	High-level design of both our overall system and the neural networks within it. Our System Architecture section and its corresponding figure illustrate how the different modules such as image-image retrieval, text-image retrieval, and the spatio-temporal filter are interconnected and work together. The term also applies to the internal structure of the deep learning models, such as the MobileNetV2 architecture, which defines how layers are organized to process visual data efficiently.

**FG-Clip** 	An improved version of the original CLIP. Focuses on fine-grained captions with the use of mult-stage training process which uses detailed, long captions and region-level information, making it better at distinguishing subtle visual features.

**Embeddings**	Are the crucial output of our deep learning models. They are dense, numerical vector representations that translate complex data like images and text into a shared mathematical space. Our FG-CLIP text encoder creates embeddings from textual descriptions, while our MobileNetV2 model creates them from images. 

**Latency**	Latency or Average and Peak Query Response Time, is a key performance metric for real-world feasibility. In our system, this measures the time delay between a user submitting a search query with text or an image and the platform returning a list of potential matches.

**Fusion**		Is the process where data from multiple modalities are combined to create a unified representation for analysis. The system performs fusion by concatenating the feature vectors (embeddings) generated from the text, image, and spatio-temporal modules.

**Tensor**		A tensor is the fundamental data structure used in deep learning to represent and manipulate data in numerical form. In image-based machine learning, tensors are used to store images, feature maps, and intermediate computations as multi-dimensional arrays.

2. ## **Methodology** {#methodology}

This section explains the methodological workflow used in building the proposed multimodal lost-and-found retrieval system. Two deep learning models are integrated: **MobileNetV2** for image-to-image retrieval and **FGCLIP** for text–image retrieval. Each model follows a distinct preprocessing pipeline, feature extraction process, and embedding workflow based on its training assumptions.

1. ### **Text-to-Image Model (FG‑CLIP Visual Similarity Retrieval Pipeline)**

FG-CLIP (Fine-Grained Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) extends the original CLIP architecture to enable more precise text-image matching through enhanced fine-grained alignment capabilities. This implementation uses the ViT-B/16 architecture variant, consisting of a Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoder and transformer-based text encoder, both producing 512-dimensional embeddings. The model is initialized with weights pretrained on CC3M and CC12M datasets.

The system processes lost item images and textual descriptions through FG‑CLIP to enable fine‑grained text-image retrieval. First, the preprocessing phase converts both images and natural‑language descriptions into standardized tensor formats that match FG‑CLIP’s pretrained vision and text encoders. Second, the architectural feature extraction stage passes the image through a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder and the text through a transformer‑based text encoder, both adapted from the CLIP architecture with fine-grained enhancements. This transforms low‑level pixels and tokens into high‑level semantic embeddings. Finally, during retrieval, the normalized image and text embeddings are compared using cosine similarity, producing a similarity score for each image-text pair so the system can rank candidates and return the images that best match the user’s description.

1. #### **Preprocessing**

The phase‑by‑phase process prepares both images and text so that they are compatible with FG‑CLIP’s dual encoders. Images are standardized in terms of resolution, channels, and normalization, while text descriptions are tokenized, padded, and given attention masks.

**Step 1: Image Loading and Conversion**

Input images are first loaded from disk using OpenCV, which decodes each file into a 3‑channel BGR (Blue, Green, Red) NumPy array. This format is incompatible with FG‑CLIP, which expects a standard RGB image. To ensure compatibility with the FG-CLIP model, the array is therefore converted from BGR to RGB using cv2.cvtColor(img\_bgr, cv2.COLOR\_BGR2RGB), reordering the memory channels of the image tensor so that index 0 is red, 1 is green, and 2 is blue. The converted NumPy array is then wrapped into a PIL.Image object with Image.fromarray, ensuring that all images share a consistent 3‑channel RGB color space that matches the convention expected by FG‑CLIP’s vision transformer.

![][image3]  
**Figure 3.2-1 Internal Logic of BGR to RGB Conversion (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-1 details the internal pixel-wise operation performed by the library function cv2.cvtColor. The function performs channel permutation. The algorithm begins by extracting spatial dimensions (height, width) from the input array and allocating a new empty array of the same size which will serve as the new RGB container. It then iterates through every vertical row (range(height)) and horizontal column (range(width)) to access each individual pixel coordinate (x, y). Inside the loop, the algorithm reads the raw channel values from the source memory. It identifies Blue at index 0, Green at index 1, and Red at index 2\. The values are written into the new array in the correct order. The red value is swapped to index 0, Green remains at index 1, and blue is swapped to index 2\. This process is repeated for every pixel in the grid, ensuring that the final returned array aligns with the RGB memory layout required by the FG-CLIP model.

**![][image4]**

**Figure 3.2-2 Internal Logic of Image Construction (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-2 details the internal object construction logic executed by the library function Image.fromarray. The algorithm begins by analyzing the input rgb\_image (produced by the algorithm in Figure 3.2-1) to extract the height, width, and number of channels. It then allocates a new, empty ImageObject in memory and sets its dimensions to match the input. Next, the logic checks the channel depth (number of channels). If it identifies 3 channels, it sets the object's mode as “RGB” allowing the system to correctly interpret the colors. The function takes the raw grid of numbers from the input array and copies them into the object's internal bitmap\_buffer, creating a new PIL image object.

![][image5]**Figure 3.2-3 RGB converted image**

Figure 3.2-3 illustrates the effect of converting an image from BGR to RGB format. The image on the left shows the original input image as read by OpenCV, which loads images in BGR channel order by default. The middle image visualizes the raw OpenCV-loaded data, highlighting that the color channels are reversed compared to standard RGB representation. The image on the right shows the result after the BGR to RGB conversion, restoring the correct color representation as expected in most image processing libraries like PIL. This conversion ensures that the red, green, and blue channels are properly interpreted, preserving the visual fidelity of the original scene when further processing or display is required.

**.Step 2: Spatial Resizing (224×224)**

Using torchvision.transforms.Resize, the RGB-converted images are then resized into a fixed spatial resolution of 224x224 pixels. This standardizes the input dimensions while preserving the overall spatial structure of the image. Internally, the resize operation does not simply stretch or crop pixel blocks. Instead, it performs spatial resampling by mapping the original image grid onto the new target grid of fixed size.

The resizing process begins by analyzing the input image dimensions and defining a new coordinate grid corresponding to the desired output resolution. For each pixel location in the 224x224 output image, the algorithm computes the corresponding fractional position in the original image. Because this position rarely aligns exactly with an original pixel, the resize operation estimates the output pixel value by interpolating nearby pixels rather than copying a single pixel. 

![][image6]  
**Figure 3.2-4 Internal Logic of Bilinear Resizing (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-4 illustrates the resizing process performed internally by the torchvision.transforms.Resize function. The algorithm accepts the pil\_img\_object (produced by the logic in Figure 3.2-2) and retrieves its source dimensions and internal bitmap\_buffer. The algorithm then determines the scaling ratio between the original image dimensions and the target 224×224 resolution. Using these ratios, each output pixel is mapped back to a fractional coordinate in the source image. The four nearest neighboring pixels surrounding this coordinate are identified, and their values are combined using distance-based weights. The bilinear interpolation is applied independently to each RGB channel, producing a smooth approximation of the original image at the new resolution. Although fine details weaken, the overall spatial structure is preserved and resized to the resolution required by FGCLIP’s vision transformer.

![][image7]**Figure 3.2-5 Resizing Image from Original Size to 224x224**

Figure 3.2-5 illustrates the resizing operation applied to the input image to meet the fixed spatial resolution required by FG-CLIP’s vision transformer. This process produces a smoother approximation of the original image at a smaller size, slightly reducing fine-grained details while preserving the overall structure, shape, and visual context of the object. The resized output ensures uniform input dimensions across all images, enabling consistent patch embedding and stable feature extraction within the model.

**Step 3: Tensor Formatting and Intensity Normalization**

After resizing as shown as figure 3.2-5 becomes the input to figure 3.2-6 for tensor conversion. The image is converted into a PyTorch tensor using transforms.ToTensor(), producing a tensor of shape \[C, H, W\], where C represents the RGB channels, and H and W are the spatial dimensions. This operation rearranges the image data from the standard image layout (H, W, C to the channel-first format (C, H, W) required by PyTorch.

During the conversion, pixel intensity values originally in the range \[0, 255\] are cast to float32 and normalized to the range \[0.0, 1.0\] by dividing by 255\. This normalization ensures consistent numerical scaling and prepares the input for subsequent model processing.

Resulting tensor shape: (3,224,224)

![][image8]

**Figure 3.2-6 Internal Logic of Tensor Conversion (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-6 details the internal data transformation performed by transforms.To.Tensor. The algorithm takes the resized\_image object (shown in Figure 3.2-5) and alters its data structure. It transposes the dimensions from the standard image format (Height, Width, Channels) to the PyTorch required format (Channels, Height, Width). It then performs type conversion and scaling. It begins by iterating through every pixel and divides the raw integer values (0-255) by 255.0. This converts them into 32-bit floating-point numbers between 0.0 and 1.0 for normalization. 

Normalization is then applied using transforms.Normalize(mean \= image\_processor.image\_mean, std=image\_processor.image\_std), Normalization follows the standard torchvision.transforms. Normalize operation, which applies Z-score standardization channel wise as: As shown in equation (3.1)

| output\[channel\] \=(input\[channel\] \- mean\[channel\])std\[channel\] | (3.1) |
| :---- | :---- |

Where mean\[channel\] and std\[channel\] are FG-CLIP’s fixed normalization constants:

* Image mean: \[0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073\]  
* Image std: \[0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711\]

This operation standardizes each channel by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation so that the input distribution matches the statistics used during FG‑CLIP pretraining. A batch dimension is then added using unsqueeze(0), resulting in a batch tensor with shape \[N, C, H, W\], where N \= batch size (number of images), C \= 3 channels (R, G, B), H \= height \= 224 pixels and W \= width \= 224 pixels. In this simulation, N \= 1 (PyTorch Contributors, n.d.), so the final batch tensor fed into the FG‑CLIP vision encoder has shape (1, 3, 224, 224). During database indexing or batch retrieval operations, multiple images can be processed simultaneously by increasing N.

![][image9]**Figure 3.2-7 Internal Logic of Normalization (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-7 details the internal element-wise operation performed by transforms.Normalize. The algorithm accepts the image\_tensor (as shown in figure 3.2-6) and iterates through the 3 color channels (Red, Green, Blue). For each channel, it retrieves the pre-calculated normalization constants. Inside the nested loops, the logic iterates through each individual pixel coordinate (x, y) in the 224x224 grid. For each pixel, it applies the formula shown in equation 3.1. It subtracts the channel mean from the scaled pixel values to center data around zero, and divides by the standard deviation to scale the variance. This produces a normalized\_tensor that matches the statistical distribution required by the FG-CLIP model.

![][image10]  
**Figure 3.2-8 Internal Logic of Batch Formatting (Pseudo-code)**

Figure 3.2-8 details the internal tensor operation performed by the unsqueeze(0) function. The algorithm accepts the normalized\_tensor (produced by the logic in Figure 3.2-7) with shape (3, 224, 224), where the dimensions correspond to color channels, height, and width. Instead of iterating over channels or pixel coordinates, the logic operates on the tensor’s structural metadata, namely its shape, dimensionality, and stride descriptors that define how the underlying data buffer is interpreted in memory. The algorithm inserts a new leading dimension of size one at index 0, representing the batch axis. Internally, this operation preserves the original contiguous memory buffer and reinterprets it as a higher-rank tensor by updating the tensor’s shape and stride descriptors. Because the newly added batch dimension has length one, all indexing operations along the axis reference the same underlying image data. The resulting tensor has shape F enabling uniform batch-based processing by the FG-CLIP vision encoder without modifying pixel values or performing additional numerical computation.

![][image11]![][image12]  
**Figure 3.2-9. Normalized-Formatted Input Image**

Figure 3.2-9 presents the normalized-formatted input image as it is represented for the FG-CLIP vision encoder. The image is shown after being structured into a batch-compatible tensor with shape (1, 3, 224, 224), ensuring consistent handling during model inference. Normalization aligns pixel value distributions across channels, allowing the encoder to process the image under a standardized numerical range while preserving the original visual content. This representation ensures compatibility with the FG-CLIP architecture without altering semantic or spatial information.

**Step 4: Text Tokenization and Padding**

The user’s natural‑language description of the lost item (for example, “brown hello kitty leather wallet”) is first converted to lowercase and passed as a Python string to FG‑CLIP’s tokenizer from the HuggingFace Transformers library. This is done by calling the tokenizer with:

tokenizer(text\_description, truncation=True, padding=”max-length”, max\_length=text\_max\_len return\_attention\_mask=true, return tensors=”pt”)

The tokenizer applies byte-pair encoding (BPE), a subword segmentation algorithm that breaks the sentence into subword units from its learned vocabulary. For each subword it then looks up a corresponding integer index, producing a 1‑D tensor of token IDs. A special beginning‑of‑sequence token \<|startoftext|\> is inserted at position 0\. Following this, the actual text description is tokenized into subword units (e.g. “brown”, “hello”, “kitty”, “leather”, “wallet”) and converted into token IDs. 

![][image13]  
**Figure 3.2-10. Internal Logic of how the Subword Units are Tokenized (Pseudocode)**

Figure 3.2-10 shows that the tokenizer splits text into subword units using Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE). Each word is processed by repeatedly finding the longest prefix that exists in the vocabulary and segmenting it until the entire word is tokenized (e.g., "kitty" → "kit" \+ "ty" ). Special tokens \<|startoftext|\> and \<|endoftext|\> are added at the beginning and end of the sequence, and each subword is converted into its corresponding integer ID from the vocabulary.

An \<|endoftext|\> token is then placed after the last content token. This token serves two roles: it marks the end of the sequence and, due to the causal attention mechanism, it acts as the final summary representation for the entire text description. Finally, PAD tokens fill all remaining positions up to the specified max\_length, ensuring uniform sequence length across the batch.

![][image14]

**Figure 3.2-11 Tokenization and ID Conversion in Text Preprocessing**

As shown in Figure 3.2-11 FG‑CLIP supports two explicit caption modes in the simulation: short‑caption mode and long‑caption mode. In short‑caption mode, the sequence is padded to a maximum length of 77 tokens including special tokens and padding, mirroring the original CLIP constraint and used for brief item descriptions. In long‑caption mode, the maximum length is increased to 248 tokens, leveraging FG‑CLIP’s extended positional embeddings so that more detailed sentences with multiple attributes can be encoded. This extended context window is particularly valuable for lost-and-found retrieval, allowing descriptions like "brown hello kitty leather wallet" without truncation. In both cases, padding is implemented by calling the tokenizer with padding="max\_length" and the chosen max\_length value. Any unused positions at the end of the sequence are filled with a dedicated PAD token ID. This ensures that every description in the batch has the same length.

![][image15]  
**Figure 3.2-12. Padding Tokens in Text Preprocessing**

Figure 3.2-12 visualizes the effect of padding on tokenized text sequences. Valid tokens occupy the initial portion of the sequence, while remaining positions are filled with padding tokens to enforce a fixed-length representation. This ensures uniform tensor dimensions across a batch, enabling efficient parallel processing while preserving the relative positions of meaningful tokens within the sequence.

**Step 5: Attention Mask Creation**

The same tokenizer call returns a second tensor in addition to input\_ids called the attention mask (return\_attention\_mask= True). For every position in the padded token sequence, the tokenizer writes a value of 1 if the position contains a real token (\<|startoftext|\>, content token, or \<|endoftext|\>) and a value of 0 if the position contains the PAD token. The first \<|endoftext|\> token is assigned a value of 1, subsequent positions after this token will be considered padding and assigned a value 0 and filled with repeated \<|endoftext|\> tokens.This produces a 1‑D PyTorch tensor of length 77 or 248 that is stored next to the token IDs. During text encoding, this attention mask is passed to the transformer so that, inside each self‑attention layer, padded positions are ignored. The model adds a large negative value to the attention logits wherever the mask is 0, so those positions receive near-zero attention weight. As a result, only meaningful tokens influence the final \<|endoftext|\> embedding. After this step both the image batch tensor and the pair of (input\_ids, attention\_mask) tensors are in the exact format required by FG‑CLIP’s dual encoders.

![][image16]  
**Figure 3.2-13. Creating Attention Mask for Tokens in Text Preprocessing**

Figure 3.2-13 illustrates the attention mask applied during text encoding, where valid tokens are marked for processing while padded positions are explicitly ignored. The mask ensures that the model attends only to meaningful token positions and excludes padding from attention computations. This prevents artificial influence from non-informative tokens and preserves the integrity of contextual relationships within the actual text content during encoding.

2. #### **Architectural Feature Extraction**

With both image as shown 3.2-9 and text inputs fully preprocessed, FG‑CLIP’s dual‑encoder architecture transforms them into semantically aligned 512‑dimensional embeddings using a pair of transformer‑based encoders.The vision encoder operates on sequences of 16×16 image patches and the text encoder operates on token sequences. Both branches rely on multi‑head self‑attention, a position‑wise Multi‑Layer Perceptron (MLP) that expands each token by a factor of 4 and projects it back to the original dimension then proceeds with GELU activation. A special CLS token to summarize global semantics for the image encoder. This token encoder aggregates information across all patches or tokens. For the vision encoder, this is the \[CLS\] token at the start, and for the text encoder, it is the \[EOS\] token at the end. Their final 512‑D outputs serve as the global image or sentence embeddings used for cross‑modal matching

**Step 1: Image Patch Embedding (Vision Encoder)**

The normalized image tensor of shape (1, 3, 224, 224\) is fed to FGCLIP's ViT-based vision encoder (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). The vision encoder consists of 12 sequential transformer blocks, each containing 12 attention heads for multi-head self-attention. Internally, the 224×224 image is divided into patches of size 16x16 pixels, which are arranged in a 14x14 grid with 196 patches total. Each 16×16 patch is a small RGB image with 3 color channels (shape 16×16×3). FGCLIP flattens each patch into a 1-D vector of length 16×16×3 \= 768 dimensions and projects it into a learned embedding space using PyTorch tensors and linear projection layers.

![][image17]  
**Figure 3.2-14. Dividing Image into a 14x14 Patch Grid**

To visualize how the image is decomposed into patches, the simulation uses PyTorch’s F.unfold operation with kernel\_size=16 and stride=16 applied to the normalized image batch. Given a 224×224 input resolution, this process divides the image into a 14×14 grid of non-overlapping patches. This extracts all 196 patches as a tensor of shape (1, 768, 196), which is then permuted to (1, 196, 768). Representative patches are displayed to demonstrate that the small 16x16 pixel regions retain meaningful visual information such as edges, textures, and color gradients. However, this unfold operation is used purely for visualization and analysis purposes. In the actual FG-CLIP inference, patch embedding is performed internally by the ViT encoder's learned linear projection layer.

![][image18]**Figure 3.2-15. Linear Projection Process**

According to figure 3.2-15 a special \[CLS\] (classification) token is prepended to the patch sequence, creating a total sequence length of 197 tokens (196 patches \+ 1 CLS token).. Positional encodings are added to each token so the encoder knows the spatial location of each patch in the original 14×14 grid. At this initial embedding stage, the \[CLS\] token represents a learned constant independent of the specific input image. It functions as an initial 'global aggregator' state that will accumulate semantic information from the patch tokens as it progresses through the Transformer's self-attention layers.

![][image19]

**Figure 3.2-16. Adding (CLS) Token and Positional Encoding**

As shown in figure 3.2-16 the sequence is then processed by the 12 transformer blocks. In each block are 12 attention heads (Vaswani et al., 2017\) for multi-head self-attention, that allow each patch token to interact with all others and gradually form a global understanding of the image. Each attention head specializes in capturing different visual patterns with some focusing on local texture relationships between adjacent patches, others on global spatial structure across the entire image. Each head achieves this by using a different fixed weight matrix from FG-CLIP’s training phase, where each numerical value was adjusted to recognize specific features and visual patterns.

For each token, the module multiplies the dimensional embedding by the weight matrix of the attention head, then computes similarity scores to every other token. Afterwards it converts these scores into attention weights with a softmax (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). The weighted sum of all other patch representations is computed so each token is updated using information from the entire image rather than its own 16x16 region (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Radford et al., 2021). The attention output at each position is passed through a position‑wise feed‑forward network (two linear layers with a GELU activation in between, applied independently to every token), consistent with the Vision Transformer architecture employed by FG-CLIP (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). The first linear layer expands the embeddings by a factor of 4, then proceeds with GELU activation. Then the second linear layer compresses it back to the original size. GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) smoothly scales each feature by a Gaussian CDF factor Φ(x), so large positive activations are mostly kept, large negative activations are almost suppressed, and mid‑range values are only partially passed. This makes the transformer more expressive and stable than using a hard ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) gate, which sets all negative values to zero (Radford et al., 2021). This network recombines and amplifies visual feature dimensions to capture higher-order patterns such as edges, textures, and object parts before passing to the next transformer block (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021).

![][image20]

**Figure 3.2-17. Evolution of Image Token Through Transformer Layers**

In figure 3.2-17, the left panel shows how the \[CLS\] token embedding evolves through 12 transformer layers, with color intensity representing activation values across the first 100 dimensions. Each row represents a successive transformer layer, showing progressive refinement of the semantic representation. The right panel displays all 197 token embeddings (1 \[CLS\] \+ 196 image patches) after the final transformer layer, revealing the spatial information encoded across different embedding dimensions.

After the final transformer block, the output at the \[CLS\] position is extracted and projected to a 512-dimensional image embedding, which will then be L2-normalized to unit length for cosine similarity computation with text embeddings during cross-modal retrieval.

Figure 3.2-18 visualizes the extracted features, represented by the \[CLS\] token embedding obtained from the transformer encoder. During self-attention, the \[CLS\] token aggregates contextual information from all patch tokens across the encoder layers. The resulting tensor has a shape of \[1, 768\], where each of the 768 dimensions corresponds to a learned latent feature capturing different semantic, structural and contextual attributes encoded by the network. It is important to note that these extracted features are numerical representations rather than explicit visual representations as once the image is processed by the encoder, FG-CLIP operates entirely on continuous numerical embeddings instead of raw image data.

**Figure 3.2-19. Numerical Extracted Features (CLS Token) \[1, 768\]**

In figure 3.2-19, the table presents the exact numerical values of selected dimensions from the same \[CLS\] token embedding in figure 3.2-18, specifically the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 768th elements of the 768-dimensional vector. 

![][image23]**Figure 3.2-20. Before and After Linear Projection \[768D → 512D\]**

**![][image24]**

**Figure 3.2-21. Internal Logic of Linear Projection \[768D → 512D\] (Pseudocode)**

Figure 3.2.21 details the code logic used to reduce the dimensionality of the text embeddings. The variable input\_768 captures the raw output vector from the transformer, explicitly identifying its shape as 768 features. The system defines the weight\_matrix, a grid of learnable parameters with shape (768, 512\) used for feature mapping. Additionally, a 1D array of shape (512) is defined as the bias\_vector, which is used to fine-tune the numerical results. The transformation occurs in the line output\_512 \= (input\_768 @ weight\_matrix) \+ bias\_vector, where the @ operator executes a matrix multiplication (dot product). This operation compresses the vector from 768 dimensions down to 512\.

**Step 2: Text Encoding (Text Encoder)**

The padded token IDs and attention masks produced during preprocessing are passed to FGCLIP's text encoder as PyTorch tensors named input\_ids and attention\_mask. The text encoder implements a transformer-based architecture consisting of 12 sequential transformer blocks, with each block containing 8 parallel attention heads for multi-head self-attention. The input accepts up to 77 tokens in short-caption mode or 248 tokens in long-caption mode (including special tokens \<|startoftext|\> and \<|endoftext|\>), where each token ID is mapped to a 512-dimensional dense embedding vector through a learned embedding matrix. Text is first tokenized using Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), a subword tokenization method that iteratively merges the most frequent pairs of characters or character sequences into a single token. This allows rare or unseen words to be represented as sequences of known subword tokens, improving the model’s ability to handle diverse vocabulary. Each resulting token ID is then mapped to a 512-dimensional dense embedding vector through a learned embedding matrix. Positional embeddings are added to these token embeddings to encode sequential position information before processing through the transformer layers.

Positional embeddings allow transformers to capture the order and structure of input data. Since transformer layers process all tokens or image patches in parallel, they do not inherently recognize sequential or spatial relationships. By adding positional embeddings to token embeddings for text and patch embeddings for images, the model encodes information about relative or absolute positions within a sequence. Internally, each position in the sequence is mapped to a dense vector, which is either learned during training or generated using a fixed function such as sinusoidal encoding. These vectors are summed with the token or patch embeddings so that each element carries both its content and positional information before entering the transformer layers. This positional information is crucial for effectively aligning textual and visual features in downstream tasks, such as image-caption matching, retrieval, and classification.

![][image25]  
**Figure 3.2-22. Input Tokens**

Figure 3.2.22 visualizes the input tokens and their sequential positions. Each bar's length corresponds to the token's position index. The tokens are displayed in the same order as they appear in the input text description.

![][image26]  
**Figure 3.2-23. Token Embedding Layer** 

Figure 3.2-23 visualizes the token embeddings extracted from the vocabulary lookup. This layer converts token IDs into 512-dimensional embedding vectors through vocabulary lookup. According to the figure, special tokens show distinctive magnitudes: \<|startoftext|\> at \~0.44 and \<|endoftext|\> padding at \~0.72, while content words maintain uniform magnitudes (\~0.28-0.30), establishing balanced semantic representations.

![][image27]  
**Figure 3.2-24. Adding Positional Encoding to Text Tokens**

As shown in Figure 3.2-24 the token embeddings are then processed by the 12 transformer blocks, where multi-head self-attention and feed-forward layers enable each word to attend to other words in the description and update its representation based on contextual relationships. Each attention head specializes in capturing different linguistic patterns, (e.g., adjective-noun pairs), others on broader semantic relationships across the sequence. The \<|endoftext|\> (EOS) token progressively aggregates information from all preceding content tokens across the layers, serving as the sentence-level representation. Because the text encoder uses causal masking (tokens can only attend to previous positions), the start token cannot 'see' the sentence. Therefore, the model relies on the End-of-Sequence token to summarize the full semantic meaning.

Similar to the vision encoder, for every token, the module first multiplies the embedding by the attention head’s weight matrix (optimized during FG-CLIP’s training) then computes similarity scores to all other tokens in the caption, turns these scores into attention weights with a softmax, and uses them to build a weighted sum of the other token representations, so each word embedding is updated using information from the entire sentence rather than just its immediate neighbors. The attention output at each position is passed through the same position‑wise feed‑forward network (two linear layers with a GELU activation in between, applied independently to every token). This re‑combines and amplifies linguistic feature dimensions to capture higher‑order patterns such as modifier–noun relationships and overall sentence semantics before the next transformer block.

![][image28]**Figure 3.2-25. Evolution of Text Token Through Transformer Layers**

In figure 3.2-25, the left panel shows how the \[EOS\] token embedding evolves through 12 transformer layers, showing progressive refinement of the first 100 embedding dimensions. The panel on the right shows all token embeddings after 12 transformer blocks, where the gradient reveals varying activation strengths across tokens and dimensions.

After the final transformer block, the output at the \<|endoftext|\> position is extracted. This specific token vector, which now contains the aggregated context of the entire description, is projected to a 512-dimensional text embedding. This 512-dimensional text embedding will then be L2-normalized to unit length for cosine similarity computation with image embeddings during cross-modal retrieval.

The resulting values along the y-axis reflect how strongly each feature is activated, which determines how the model “understands” the \[eos\] token in context.

**Step 3: L2 Normalization Process**

Following the standard practice for Clip-based models (Radford et al., 2021\) the raw 512-dimensional feature vectors returned by get\_image\_features() and get\_text\_features() are explicitly L2-normalized before similarity computation so that their lengths are equal to one. As a result, all embeddings are normalized to the same scale, which means that when comparing embeddings, only the direction of each vector matters, not its magnitude. This makes cosine similarity equivalent to the dot product and ensures that only the direction of each embedding affects similarity scoring (Xie et al., 2025\) 

| v \=v|| v ||2 | (3.2) |
| :---- | :---- |

Compact formula for L2 normalization

Where:  
v \= original 512-D feature vector  
||v||2 \= its L2 norm (Euclidean Length)  
v \= L2 normalized vector, same direction, length 1

Vector components: (v1 ,  v2 ,   v3 ,  ... v512)

1. Length

| || v ||2 \= v12+ v22+ ...  v5122 | (3.3) |
| :---- | :---- |

2. Normalize: divide every component by that length

| vi \=vi|| v ||2 | (3.4) |
| :---- | :---- |

Essentially, L2 normalization divides each component of the 512-D feature vector by its L2 norm (Euclidean Length), so the resulting vector length is 1\.

In the simulation, this L2 normalization is implemented using torch.nn.functional.normalize(feature\_vector, p=2, dim=1), where p \= 2 specifies the L2 norm and dim=1 indicates normalization across the 512 feature dimensions, applied separately to both the image embedding returned by model.get\_image\_features(pixel\_values) and text embedding returned by model.get\_text\_features(input\_ids, attention\_mask).
